ad-astra-per-aspera-motivation-tracker.title: Use a Short Phrase to Choose the Next Step
ad-astra-per-aspera-motivation-tracker.description: Use a brief phrase as a cue to acknowledge a difficult moment and choose one small, controllable action. The phrase is a reminder, not a prediction about how the situation will end.
ad-astra-per-aspera-motivation-tracker.reason: Replace an inherited motivation article containing fabricated pilot outcomes, percentages, physiological explanations, rigid repetition targets and app-first promotion with a bounded reflection-and-action cue.
forbidden_public_fragments: median reduction 1–2 minutes in pilot settings
Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Choose one brief phrase that helps you acknowledge difficulty without pretending it is useful or deserved. Use it as a cue to identify one small action you can control.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: When you feel stuck, pause and repeat a short phrase once. Name what is difficult in plain language, then choose one action that is small enough to begin now. Skip the phrase if it feels hollow, pressuring or unrelated to the real problem.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What was difficult, what action did I choose, and did the phrase help me begin or should I use a different cue next time?

faq.question: Do I need to use the Latin phrase?
faq.answer: No. Use plain language if it feels more honest. A useful cue should help you notice the situation and choose an action, not impress you with its wording.

faq.question: What if the phrase feels dismissive?
faq.answer: Drop it. Some difficulties need rest, support, a boundary, a changed plan or professional help rather than a motivational line.

faq.question: What should I track?
faq.answer: Record the situation, the next action you chose and whether you started it. The useful signal is what happened after the cue, not how many times you repeated it.

intro.html: A short phrase can act as a transition between feeling stuck and choosing what to do next. It does not make hardship meaningful and it does not solve the underlying problem. Use it only when it helps you face the situation clearly and begin one controllable action.

sections.title: 1. Choose a grounded phrase
sections.html: Use Ad astra per aspera, one step at a time, or another line that feels credible to you. Avoid language that demands constant toughness or treats suffering as a requirement for success.

sections.title: 2. Name what is difficult
sections.html: Describe the immediate problem without turning it into an identity statement: I do not know how to start this draft, I need to ask for help, or this plan no longer fits.

sections.title: 3. Choose one controllable action
sections.html: Pick the smallest action that changes the situation: open the document, write the question, move the deadline, contact the person, take a real break, or decide that continuing is not the right move.

sections.title: 4. Review whether the cue helped
sections.html: After the action, note whether the phrase helped you begin, made no difference, or added pressure. Keep it only if it supports clearer action.

sections.title: 5. Do not use a motto to override a boundary
sections.html: A phrase should not persuade you to remain in an unsafe, harmful or pointless situation. Change the plan, seek support or stop when that is the more responsible action.

analogy-studio.title: Explain One Idea with an Analogy and Its Limit
analogy-studio.description: Compare an unfamiliar idea with something familiar, state the matching point, name where the comparison stops and ask the listener to restate the idea.
analogy-studio.reason: Replace an inherited NLP-branded article containing invented comprehension, recall and laboratory statistics with a neutral communication practice that tests an analogy through listener paraphrase and explicit boundaries.
forbidden_public_fragments: improved comprehension in pilot trials by about 40%
recalled at a rate of 55–70% after 24 hours
60% to 84% in lab runs of 120 attempts
Their paraphrases missed the main mechanism 40% of the time
Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Explain one unfamiliar idea by comparing it with something the listener already knows, then state the exact point of comparison and where the analogy stops.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Write the idea you need to explain. Choose a familiar comparison, map only the important relationship, add one boundary sentence and ask the listener to restate the original idea. Revise the analogy if the restatement keeps the wrong detail.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Could the listener restate the intended idea, and which part of the analogy clarified or distorted it?

faq.question: How do I know whether an analogy is useful?
faq.answer: Ask the listener to explain the original idea in their own words. A memorable comparison is not useful if it preserves the wrong relationship.

faq.question: What if the listener takes the analogy literally?
faq.answer: State the boundary directly: explain which part matches and which part does not. Replace the analogy when the boundary needs more explanation than the idea itself.

faq.question: Should I use the same analogy for every audience?
faq.answer: No. Choose a familiar source for the specific listener and avoid comparisons that carry distracting, loaded or misleading associations.

intro.html: An analogy can make a structure easier to see, but it also imports assumptions from the familiar example. The practice is not merely to invent a vivid comparison. It is to map one useful relationship, expose the limit and check what the listener understood.

sections.title: 1. Define the idea you need to explain
sections.html: Write one sentence describing the target idea without an analogy. This gives you something to compare the listener's later restatement against.

sections.title: 2. Choose a familiar source
sections.html: Pick an object, activity or system the listener already understands. Familiarity matters more than cleverness. A comparison from their work or daily life is usually easier to inspect than an ornate metaphor.

sections.title: 3. Map the important relationship
sections.html: Say what corresponds to what. Keep only the relationship needed for the explanation, such as flow through a bottleneck, temporary storage or repeated practice.

sections.title: 4. State where the analogy stops
sections.html: Add a short boundary such as the comparison only describes the flow, not the underlying mechanism. This prevents a useful shortcut from becoming a false model.

sections.title: 5. Test the listener's paraphrase
sections.html: Ask the listener to restate the original idea rather than repeat the metaphor. If the wrong detail survives, revise the mapping or choose a different comparison.

ask-better-interview-questions.title: Run a Short, Concrete Information Interview
ask-better-interview-questions.description: Ask permission, focus on one recent event, follow the sequence step by step and separate remembered facts, estimates and interpretation.
ask-better-interview-questions.reason: Replace an inherited interview guide containing unsupported multipliers, sample claims, fabricated observations and arbitrary precision with a consent-based protocol for gathering concrete, correctable information.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form
We remember asking the same follow-up three times

lifeOsSource.hack: Ask about one recent real event, follow it in sequence and check your summary with the other person before treating it as information.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Explain why you are asking and get permission. Ask the person to walk through the most recent relevant example. Use one question at a time about sequence, context, tools, decisions and uncertainty. Summarize what you heard and invite correction.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What concrete sequence did I learn, what remains an estimate or interpretation, and what did the person correct?

faq.question: How do I keep the conversation from feeling like an interrogation?
faq.answer: Explain the purpose, ask permission, keep the scope narrow and let the person skip a question. Curiosity does not cancel consent.

faq.question: What should I do with a vague answer?
faq.answer: Ask for the most recent example and one step at a time. Accept uncertainty instead of forcing a precise number or explanation the person cannot recall.

faq.question: How do I avoid misquoting the person?
faq.answer: Summarize the sequence and key distinction back to them, then invite correction. Keep facts, estimates and your interpretation labelled separately.

intro.html: A useful interview produces a concrete, correctable account rather than an impressive pile of questions. Start with one recent event, move through it in sequence and check that your notes match what the person meant.

sections.title: 1. Set the purpose and ask permission
sections.html: State what you are trying to understand and how the information will be used. Ask whether the person is comfortable discussing the example and respect any boundary they set.

sections.title: 2. Choose one recent example
sections.html: Ask about the last relevant event rather than the person's general theory of what usually happens. A specific example gives both of you something concrete to inspect.

sections.title: 3. Follow the sequence one step at a time
sections.html: Begin with what happened first? and continue with the next step. Ask separately about context, tools, handoffs, decisions and workarounds instead of combining several questions.

sections.title: 4. Label facts, estimates and interpretations
sections.html: When the person is unsure, record the answer as an estimate. Keep your inference separate from what they directly described, especially when interpreting motives or causes.

sections.title: 5. Summarize and invite correction
sections.html: Repeat the sequence and the important distinction in your own words. Ask what you missed or misunderstood before using the notes to make a decision.

ask-for-feedback-tracker.title: Ask for Feedback on One Specific Decision
ask-for-feedback-tracker.description: Give the reviewer context, ask one focused question, make the reply easy and decide what you will accept, test, discuss, defer or ignore.
ask-for-feedback-tracker.reason: Replace an inherited Dunning-Kruger and feedback article containing fabricated internal trials, cohort outcomes, response-rate claims and arbitrary quotas with a bounded feedback request and review protocol.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Ask for feedback on one concrete artifact or decision, using a question the reviewer can answer from relevant experience.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: State the intended outcome and the current decision. Ask one focused question such as what is unclear, what assumption looks wrong or what should change first. Choose a reviewer who can judge that question, then record what you will accept, test, discuss, defer or ignore.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What did I ask, what did the reviewer actually say, and what decision or test changed because of it?

faq.question: What if reviewers disagree?
faq.answer: Compare each comment with the intended outcome and ask for the reasoning behind the difference. You may need a small test or a decision from the accountable owner rather than a vote.

faq.question: Do I need to accept every comment?
faq.answer: No. Feedback is information, not an instruction. Record why you accepted, tested, discussed, deferred or rejected it.

faq.question: How often should I ask?
faq.answer: Ask at useful decision points, when the cost of being wrong matters or when another perspective can reveal a blind spot. Avoid a quota that creates requests with no clear purpose.

intro.html: Feedback is easier to use when the reviewer knows the intended outcome and the decision you are making. Ask one question that fits their experience, then turn the response into an explicit decision rather than collecting comments indefinitely.

sections.title: 1. Choose one decision or artifact
sections.html: Use a draft, slide, design, message, plan or piece of work that can still change. State the intended audience and outcome so the reviewer knows what standard to apply.

sections.title: 2. Ask one focused question
sections.html: Replace any thoughts? with a question such as what is unclear?, which assumption would you challenge?, or what should change before this is ready?

sections.title: 3. Choose a relevant reviewer
sections.html: Ask someone who understands the audience, domain, decision or implementation constraint. A senior title does not automatically make feedback relevant.

sections.title: 4. Separate the signal from the delivery
sections.html: Pause before editing. Identify the concrete observation, the reviewer's interpretation and any proposed change. A harsh tone can contain a useful signal, and a kind tone can still contain a weak suggestion.

sections.title: 5. Record what changes
sections.html: Choose an explicit disposition: accept, test, discuss, defer or reject. Note the reason and the next action so the feedback loop ends in a decision rather than a growing comment archive.
